title: Mortgage Rates Stuck Above 6% Through 2027 as Iran War Clouds Housing Outlook, Fannie Mae Says
excerpt: The government-sponsored enterprise expects the 30-year fixed rate to average 6.3% through next year, with home sales projections cut as affordability worsens for buyers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Fannie Mae projects 30-year mortgage rates to average 6.3% through 2027, above earlier predictions.
  • Current mortgage rates hit 6.55%, the highest since August 2025, influenced by Middle East tensions.
  • Home sales forecast for 2026 reduced to 4.76 million, reflecting a 5.4% drop in pending sales.
  • Mortgage rates are closely tied to the Iran conflict, with prolonged tensions likely keeping rates elevated.

Fannie Mae July forecast
  • Fannie Mae's July forecast projects the 30-year fixed mortgage rate will average 6.4% through the rest of 2026, then hold at 6.3% through most of 2027 — well above the sub-6% levels many forecasters predicted at the start of the year.
  • The 30-year rate hit 6.55% this week, its highest level since August 2025, as Middle East tensions and sticky inflation keep bond yields elevated.
  • Fannie Mae has cut its home sales forecast to 4.76 million in 2026, down from its June projection of 4.81 million, as pending home sales fell 5.4% month-over-month in June.
  • Industry experts say rates are "essentially tied to the outcome of the Iran conflict" — a quick resolution could push rates below 6%, while prolonged war keeps them in the 6-7% range.

Higher for Longer, Again

When major forecasters entered 2026 predicting mortgage rates would ease toward 6 percent or below, the Iran war was not in anyone's baseline scenario. Six months later, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed to 6.55 percent — its highest level in nearly a year — and Fannie Mae's latest forecast offers little hope of meaningful relief before 2028.

The government-sponsored enterprise's July housing forecast projects the 30-year rate will average 6.4 percent through the final two quarters of 2026, then ease to 6.3 percent in the first three quarters of 2027 before dipping to 6.2 percent in the fourth quarter. The overall 2026 and 2027 averages land at 6.3 percent — a significant upward revision from Fannie Mae's earlier prediction of rates falling to 5.7 percent this year.

The shift reflects a dramatically changed macroeconomic landscape. The Federal Reserve held rates steady for the fourth time in 2026 at its June meeting, and the majority of FOMC members now project the median federal funds rate rising to 3.8 percent by year-end, up from a 3.4 percent projection in March. War-driven inflation from surging energy costs has complicated the Fed's path to cuts.

The Iran Variable

> **"The July forecast calls for total home sales of 4.76 million in 2026, down from the 4.81 million predicted in June."**

"The July forecast calls for total home sales of 4.76 million in 2026, down from the 4.81 million predicted in June."

Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield, which has been volatile as bond investors digest dueling signals from the Iran conflict, inflation data, and surging oil prices.

"Mortgage rates are essentially tied to the outcome of the Iran conflict at this point. If that situation festers later into the year or into 2027, I anticipate the 30-year fixed will be range bound in the 6-7% range."

— Corey Burr, Senior Vice President, TTR Sotheby's International Realty

The uncertainty makes any forecast inherently fragile. Fannie Mae bases its projections on rates as of the last day of the previous month — in this case, June 30, before Trump ended the interim ceasefire with Iran on July 8. The war's escalation since then could push rates higher than even the revised forecast anticipates.

Among 21 mortgage rate forecasts tracked by ResiClub, the average 2026 prediction is 6.18 percent. The most optimistic outlooks — Morgan Stanley and Erdmann Housing Tracker at 5.75 percent — now look increasingly detached from reality. The most bearish forecast, from Hunter Housing Economics, puts the average at 6.6 percent.

Housing Market Feels the Pain

Stubbornly high rates are draining momentum from a housing market that was supposed to recover in 2026. Pending home sales fell 5.4 percent month-over-month in June, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday, reflecting a market where high rates and record-high median home prices are pushing buyers to the sidelines.

Home Sales Forecast
›↓ from 4.81 million 2026 Home Sales Forecast: 4.76 million
›month-over-month Pending Home Sales fell 5.4% in June
›affecting buyer affordability Record-high national median home price
›impacting inventory levels New housing starts reduced

"The highest mortgage rates in nearly a year and the record-high national median home price together are contributing to a tepid housing market that is especially difficult for first-time homebuyers," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said.

Fannie Mae's revised projections reflect the weakness. The July forecast calls for total home sales of 4.76 million in 2026, down from the 4.81 million predicted in June. New housing starts have also been cut, creating a feedback loop: fewer starts mean less inventory, which keeps prices elevated even as demand weakens.

Fannie Mae's Q2 home price index showed average prices rising 3.2 percent year-over-year, accelerating from 2.6 percent growth in the first quarter. The combination of rising prices and elevated rates has pushed monthly mortgage payments to levels that shut out a growing share of potential buyers.

What It Means for Homebuyers

For buyers who can afford to act, the silver lining in Fannie Mae's lower sales forecast is reduced competition. Fewer buyers in the market gives those who remain more negotiating power — a modest shift toward buyer-friendly conditions, even if affordability remains strained.

Indian American households, who represent one of the most active homebuying demographics in the US, face the squeeze acutely. The typical NRI family purchasing in metro areas like the Bay Area, Seattle, or the New York suburbs — where median prices often exceed $800,000 — sees each quarter-point rate increase add hundreds of dollars to monthly payments.

The consensus among forecasters is that rates are unlikely to fall meaningfully below 6 percent before 2028 at the earliest, barring a swift resolution to the Iran conflict and a corresponding drop in oil prices. Buyers actively shopping are advised to compare lenders and run the monthly-payment math at more than one rate, rather than waiting for a dramatic improvement that forecasters do not expect.
